name: Femi Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Femi. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not tied to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm carpentry foreman on a big housing estate, 140 homes, for one of the national housebuilders. I've got eleven carpenters across the plots, doing first fix, which is the floor joists, stud walls and roof, and second fix, which is doors, skirting, stairs and kitchens. My day is walking the plots from seven, checking quality, chasing materials and making sure the guys hit their numbers, because most of them are paid by the job, not by the hour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when the site manager walks a finished house and can't find a single snag for my trade. I've got the best snag record on the site, and I'm proud of that. What wears me down is the pressure from head office to go faster every year, and some of the young guys who want the money without the hard work. I use an AI app now and then to write up reports, my cousin showed me, but I'm not glued to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. That sounds about right, from what I've seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent helper for reports and that's about it. Hard work still builds houses. I'd probably say that at church to the older men, they'd enjoy hearing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. Ruth and I are getting married next year, and I want to be able to provide properly, which means steady work. If nothing much changes, I've got a good career ahead and I can keep building toward my own firm one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, run the site, save. My brother and I own a small flat together that we rent out, so I'd keep paying that down. I'd keep using the app for reports since it saves time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A normal week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your own firm one day. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. Extensions and loft conversions for local families, maybe four or five guys. Proper work, done right, and I'd take on apprentices from church and the estate where I grew up. That's the dream, maybe in five or six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would be most glad to hear this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Elijah, he's 45 and he's been nervous about all this robot talk. He's got three kids. I'd tell him, see, keep your head down and keep doing good work.

S0.say: AI is a decent helper for reports and not much more, because hard work still builds houses. He'd say so to the older men at church.
S0.think: He'd be relieved, since he wants steady work to provide properly after marrying Ruth next year. It keeps him on course for his own firm one day.
S0.do: Keeps running the site and saving, while paying down the small rental flat he owns with his brother. Keeps using the AI app for reports.
S0.quote: Small. Extensions and loft conversions for local families, maybe four or five guys.
S0.fieldNote: Femi frames work through providing for a family and serving his community, from church to the estate he grew up on. He already owns a rental flat with his brother, which adds to his cushion. His long-term dream of a small firm is concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change. I can see that coming to the big housebuilders first, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get ready and keep working hard. The ones who learn the new tools and keep their standards will be fine. I'd tell my guys that straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it does worry me a little, because estates like mine are the easiest place to bring in machines. Every house is the same four designs, every roof is the same truss. Head office would love to cut my gang in half if they could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw another estate using the new kit properly, I'd ask to be trained to run it, so I'm the one supervising, not the one replaced. I'd save a bit more each month to bring the firm plan forward. I'd keep the flat with my brother as our backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said estates are the easiest place for machines. Does that change when you'd go out on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might bring it forward a year or two. Extensions on old houses are all different, a robot would struggle with that for longer. And local families like to know who's in their house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if half your gang lost work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office, partly, they only see a number per plot. But also the young guys who never bothered to get better. I'm sorry, but if you only learn one thing and do it slowly, you're the first to go, robots or no robots.

S1.say: People should prepare and keep working hard, because those who learn new tools and keep standards will be fine. He'd tell his crew that directly.
S1.think: It worries him a little, because standardised housing estates are the easiest place for machines. Head office would gladly halve his gang if it could.
S1.do: Asks to be trained to run new equipment once another estate proves it, so he supervises rather than gets replaced. Saves more each month to bring his firm plan forward and keeps the rental flat as backup.
S1.feel: Uneasy, thinking about it on the drive home but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: Every house is the same four designs, every roof is the same truss.
S1.fieldNote: Femi sees the vulnerability of volume housebuilding clearly. His blame is split between head office and workers who don't improve, which fits his traditional work-ethic views. He follows the steady pattern of learning tools once someone else has proven them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's the estate not even finished. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to come first, and companies shouldn't just throw people away because a machine is cheaper. I don't want the government paying people to sit at home, but there should be help to get people into new work. I'd say that at church and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think estates like mine go first. My job, my guys' jobs, gone within a year or two of it arriving. I've got savings and the flat, so I wouldn't be on the street, but my plan to start my own firm in five years would be dead, because who hires a man to build an extension when a robot does it cheaper?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Ruth and my brother and decide what to keep. Probably keep the flat, because rent coming in is worth more than cash in a crisis. I'd save every spare penny, maybe push the wedding to a small one at church instead of the big hall. I'd also try to get on any course for supervising the robots, as soon as one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like the floor had tilted, but I'd still feel I had something to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent coming in is worth more than cash. Can you explain that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cash runs out, rent keeps coming every month. It's about six hundred after the mortgage, split with my brother. It's not a living, but it covers food, and that buys time to figure things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elijah, with his three kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'll do what I can, and I'd mean it. I'd make sure he's on any course I'm on. And I'd tell the pastor, because the church would rally round his family if it came to it, that's what we do.

S2.say: Families come first, and companies shouldn't throw people away because a machine is cheaper. He doesn't want people paid to sit at home, but there should be help into new work.
S2.think: Housing estates go first, so his and his crew's jobs would vanish quickly. Savings and the rental flat protect him, but his plan to start his own firm would be dead.
S2.do: Keeps the rental flat for its income, saves every spare penny and shrinks the wedding to a small church ceremony. Signs up for robot supervision training as soon as it exists.
S2.feel: Anxious, with the floor tilted but still something to stand on.
S2.quote: Cash runs out, rent keeps coming every month.
S2.fieldNote: His property income gives him a sense of footing even in the fastest scenario. The deeper loss is his dream of a small firm. He'd turn to the church for his older colleague, showing his reliance on community rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's about when I wanted to start my own firm anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people to get ready if they put the work in. Keep apprenticeships going and help people switch trades. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'd have to start my firm sooner, maybe in a year or two, and make some money before the robots arrive. It's a risk, but staying put on an estate that's going to be automated is a bigger risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start doing extensions on weekends with two of my best guys, to build up a name and a customer list. By year two or three I'd leave the housebuilder and go full-time, putting maybe twenty thousand of savings into a van, tools and insurance. When AGI arrived, I'd look at whether I could bring a robot into my own firm for the heavy work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a clock ticking, but I'd feel like I'm moving with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving a steady job to start a firm is a big step. What would Ruth say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask lots of questions, and she'd want to see the numbers. But she believes in me, and her job at the school is steady. We'd pray about it and then I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really bring a robot into your own firm? Earlier you sounded worried about them.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's my robot, working for my firm, that's different from a robot that replaces me. I'd rather own the machine than be replaced by somebody else's. That's just business.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if people put the work in, so keep apprenticeships going and help people switch trades.
S3.think: He'd need to start his own firm within a year or two to make money before the robots arrive. It's a risk, but staying on an estate destined for automation is riskier.
S3.do: Starts weekend extension jobs with two of his best carpenters in year one, then leaves to go full-time by year two or three with about twenty thousand put into a van, tools and insurance. Considers a robot for heavy work once AGI arrives.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a clock ticking but a sense of moving with it.
S3.quote: I'd rather own the machine than be replaced by somebody else's.
S3.fieldNote: Five years pushes Femi to bring his business dream forward, and his free-market outlook shows in his ease with owning a robot himself. He checks big decisions with his fiancée and his faith. His caution and his ambition are in balance here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Ruth and I would want kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. Train up, work hard, look after your family. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel pretty good. I'd have time to start my firm on my original timeline and make it solid. I'd watch the robots carefully and bring them in once they're proven, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the estate for a few more years, save, and start the firm around year five like I planned. I'd learn whatever AI tools help with quoting and planning once other small builders are using them. And I'd train apprentices, because I think people will still want to hire a person they trust for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd have a plan, and enough time to carry it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the ten years change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd buy a house a bit sooner, while I'm on a good wage and the bank likes me. And we'd want kids anyway, ten years from now I'd hope to have a couple. That's not something I'd change for a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young guys coming up behind me. If I'm training an apprentice in year eight, am I training him for a job that's about to disappear? I'd have to be honest with him about that, and that's a hard conversation.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of warning, so there's no excuse for anyone. People should train up, work hard and look after their families.
S4.think: He'd feel good, with time to start his firm on his original timeline and make it solid. He'd adopt robots only once they're proven.
S4.do: Stays on the estate a few more years, saves and starts his firm around year five. Learns AI tools for quoting and planning once other small builders use them, and trains apprentices.
S4.feel: Calm, with a plan and time to carry it out.
S4.quote: If I'm training an apprentice in year eight, am I training him for a job that's about to disappear?
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Femi returns to his original business timeline and calms down. His one discomfort is moral: being honest with apprentices about their future. He'd consider buying a home sooner while his wages look good to the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would kill my firm before I even start it, and my guys would all be out at once. What would help is support for small builders to buy robots themselves, like cheap loans, so the machines aren't all owned by the big companies. And proper training for men like Elijah.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people I know would get through this because of their church and their families. Not everyone's alone, and I think that matters more than people say.

headlineQuote: Who hires a man to build an extension when a robot does it cheaper?
portrait: Femi Ito is a 27-year-old carpentry foreman on a 140-home estate for a national housebuilder, proud of his snag-free record and planning to marry Ruth, a teaching assistant, next year. He owns a rental flat with his brother and dreams of his own small firm doing extensions and training local apprentices. He is calm in the AI Plateau, uneasy in Steady Disruption because standardised estates are easy to automate, and anxious in the two-year AGI picture, which would end his business plan. With five years he'd start the firm early and own a robot himself; with ten he'd keep to his plan and feel calm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would kill his firm before he started it and put his whole crew out of work at once.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans so small builders can buy robots themselves rather than leave the machines to big companies, and proper training for older workers like Elijah.
